metadata.title: One Model, Three Numbers
metadata.subject: Optimizing smaller models for coding with agentic systems and RL
metadata.primary_source: Together AI / Agentica — DeepSWE-Preview (Qwen3-32B, RL only); Yang et al., SWE-smith (SWE-agent-LM-32B)
metadata.note: ai-explainer spine, claude-hai channel, Weekly STEM. FRAMEWORK: three questions for any coding-agent score — ONE RUN OR BEST OF N / WHICH SCAFFOLD AND HOW MUCH CONTEXT / WHO PICKED THE WINNER. Falsifiability beat is B06: the DeepSWE comparison table mixes four scaffolds and three test-time settings across ten rows, so reading it as a leaderboard is unsupported — and B05 shows the authors' own table has a SMALLER model (Devstral-Small 24B, 46.6) above DeepSWE on one attempt. Every figure taken from the primary source, not from aggregator pages. See FACTCHECK.md.

render.note: 4K-native sources: Manim at 2160p24, Remotion at scale 2.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane. If you want to make a small model good at coding, the literature gives you two levers — reinforcement learning, and the agent you wrap around it. The published numbers mix them together, and one open model reports three different scores on the same benchmark.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the topic question, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the topic question and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "how much of a small coding model's score is the model, and how much is the agent around it?"
props.segment: Uday Sonawane · One Model, Three Numbers
output: the scaffold is doing real work

beats.role_note: the whole reel in one image — three published numbers for one model on one benchmark
beats.narration_text: Here is the thing to look at. DeepSWE-Preview is a thirty-two billion parameter open model trained with reinforcement learning. On SWE-bench Verified it scores forty-two point two. It also scores fifty-nine. It also scores seventy-one. Same model, same five hundred problems, same week. Those are not three attempts at one measurement. They are three different measurements, and only one of them is something you can ship.
beats.new_visual_element: the three scores, side by side, before any explanation

shot.visual_intent: Three bordered stat cards in a row, each with a large figure. All three are soft ink except the first, which is terracotta. No captions yet beyond the benchmark name — the beat is the discomfort of three numbers with no labels.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions for any coding-agent score, AS A STRUCTURE before the evidence
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any coding-agent score. One: one run, or best of N — because best-of-N is a different product. Two: which scaffold, and how much context — the harness is not neutral. Three: who picked the winner — a verifier you can actually run, or an oracle that already knows the answer. The third one is where most of the inflation lives.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: ONE RUN OR BEST OF N / WHICH SCAFFOLD / WHO PICKED THE WINNER
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The third lands in terracotta — it is the question that separates 59 from 71, and the rest of the reel is scored against all three.

beats.role_note: what the RL recipe actually is — so 'trained with RL' stops being a slogan
beats.narration_text: First, what was actually done. The base is Qwen3-32B. The training is reinforcement learning only — no distillation from a stronger model, which matters because most open coding models are fine-tuned on traces from something bigger. The algorithm is a modified GRPO. Forty-five hundred real software tasks, with every repository that appears in the benchmark filtered out of training first. Sixty-four H100s, six days.

shot.show: base model, method, task count, decontamination, compute
shot.visual_intent: A bordered panel on the left lists the recipe as monospace rows. On the right, a small bordered card isolates the decontamination step in terracotta, because it is the one that makes the score mean anything. Citation strip names the model card.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 1 — the three numbers decomposed, with what each one actually measures
beats.narration_text: Now the three numbers. Forty-two point two is pass-at-one, averaged over sixteen runs — that is one attempt, which is what a user gets. Fifty-seven point nine is best of eight. Fifty-nine is best of sixteen, with a verifier choosing between them. And seventy-one is also best of sixteen, but chosen by an oracle that already knows which patch passes. That last one is an upper bound on the method. It is not a result you can deploy.
beats.new_visual_element: the four scores with their measurement labels attached

shot.show: 42.2 one run / 57.9 best@8 / 59.0 best@16 verifier / 71.0 best@16 oracle
shot.visual_intent: Four horizontal bars, proportional, each with its figure at the right and a monospace label beneath naming what it measures. The oracle bar is drawn with a dashed border to mark that it is not shippable. Citation strip names the model card and the benchmark.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 2 — the scaffold, using the paper's OWN comparison table against itself
beats.narration_text: Question two, the scaffold. In the same table the authors published, Devstral-Small scores forty-six point six on one attempt. That is four points above DeepSWE's forty-two point two, from a model eight billion parameters smaller. The difference is not obviously the model. One runs on OpenHands, the other on R2E-Gym, with a sixty-four thousand token window and a hundred steps. Change the harness and the number moves.
beats.new_visual_element: the smaller model with the higher single-run score

shot.show: Devstral-Small 24B at 46.6 against DeepSWE 42.2, with scaffolds named
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered cards side by side. Left: DeepSWE-Preview, 32B, R2E-Gym, 42.2. Right: Devstral-Small, 24B, OpenHands, 46.6, in terracotta. Beneath, a monospace line notes 64k context and 100 steps. Citation strip names the comparison table.

beats.role_note: the table is not a leaderboard — four scaffolds and three test-time settings in ten rows
beats.narration_text: This is the part that breaks the usual reading. That comparison table has ten rows and four different scaffolds in it, and three different test-time settings. Some rows are one attempt. Some are best of eight. Ranking them top to bottom produces a leaderboard that does not exist. The authors are not hiding this — the scaffold is a column in their own table. Almost nobody quoting the fifty-nine reads that column.
beats.new_visual_element: the same table, with the scaffold column made the point

shot.show: six rows with model, scaffold and setting, showing the mixture
shot.visual_intent: A table-like stack of bordered rows: model name, scaffold chip, setting chip, score. The scaffold chips use three distinct outline treatments so the mixture is visible at a glance. The two rows that are best-of-N carry a terracotta setting chip. Citation strip names the table.

beats.role_note: the other road — distillation — and which lever actually moved the number
beats.narration_text: There is a second road, and it is worth the comparison. SWE-smith generated fifty thousand training tasks across a hundred and twenty-eight repositories and fine-tuned on expert trajectories rather than using reinforcement learning. Its model scores forty point two on one attempt. Reinforcement learning scored forty-two point two. Two points apart. Meanwhile, turning on best-of-sixteen moved the same model by nearly seventeen. The training method is not where the big number came from.
beats.new_visual_element: the two training roads, then the lever that actually moved it

shot.visual_intent: Two small bordered cards at the top showing the two training approaches and their single-run scores, with a 2.0 delta chip between them. Beneath, a wider terracotta bar labelled +16.8 spanning from 42.2 to 59.0, visibly dwarfing the gap above it. Citation strip names both sources.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 3 scored, then the two-sided verdict with the cost attached
beats.narration_text: Scored. One run or best of N: three of the four published numbers are best-of-N. Which scaffold: four of them in one table. Who picked the winner: a verifier for fifty-nine, an oracle for seventy-one. So — be excited that a thirty-two billion parameter open model, trained with reinforcement learning and no distillation, does real work on real repositories. Be sceptical of any single number quoted without its scaffold and its N. And if you do want the fifty-nine, budget for it: best of sixteen means sixteen times the inference.
beats.new_visual_element: the rubric scored, then the two-sided verdict and the cost

shot.show: three rubric rows answered, then BE EXCITED ABOUT / BE SCEPTICAL OF / and the cost line
shot.visual_intent: Three label-and-chip rows score the rubric. Beneath, two lines: BE EXCITED ABOUT in ink, BE SCEPTICAL OF in terracotta. A third bordered card isolates the cost: 16x inference for best-of-16.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric on the next model card, with GOOD/BAD
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time a coding model posts a number, find three things before you believe it: the scaffold, the N, and who chose the winner. If the model card does not say, that is your answer.

shot.show: the composer with the handoff prompt and a GOOD/BAD discriminator

props.command: claude "for this coding benchmark score: name the scaffold, the context window, whether it is pass@1 or best-of-N, and who selected the winning trajectory"
props.segment: Your turn · scaffold, N, and who chose
output: GOOD: names all three, or says they are missing
BAD: “beats GPT-class models” with no harness
an oracle score is an upper bound, not a result
